source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on the SE-facing slope of a drumlin. The remains of a circular stone-built structure (int. diam. 5m N-S; 5.1m E-W). The wall survives as internal and external facing of limestone slabs, just one course high, with an earth and rubble core (T 1.25m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.35m). The entrance (Wth 0.95m) is at S. Two possible fulachtaí fia (SL039-111001-; SL039-111002-) lie c. 20m and 40m to NE and SW, respectively.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a small isolated patch of unreclaimed bog in rolling pasture about 5km W of the N end of Lough Gara. The tomb, much of which is either missing or remains concealed in the bog, faces W and protrudes from a heel-shaped mound (L 9m E-W; max. Wth 7.5m at W). The forward 2.6m of the gallery is visible. Opposed stones, 1.45m apart, form the gallery entrance. A single sidestone adjoins the southern of these and 0.6m beyond this a partly concealed stone may be a fallen orthostat. Two orthostats adjoin the northern entrance stone. Outside these there are two stones that serve to double the gallery wall at this point. A lintel that covered the entrance has slipped off the S side of the gallery. Broken lines of outer-walling to the N and S join a facade running across the W end of the tomb. Two facade-stones link the S side of the gallery entrance to the outer-wall and these articulate with a line of three outer-wall stones, each of which has fallen outwards. The surviving facade-stone at the N articulates with the front of the outer-walling at this side of the monument. It adjoins a line of five stones, the middle three fallen outwards and the easternmost partly buried. Another outer-wall stone stands some 2.3m to the E. A small set stone 2.3m S of the last is of uncertain function. Three displaced stones lie on the mound at the NE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 78-9, no. 125)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Thirteen Early Christian slabs and a slab rough-out were found in various locations around Carrowntemple graveyard (SL044-056002-), mainly to the S and E of the church (SL044-056001-), and were described by Wallace and Timoney (1987, 43-61). Nine of the thirteen are cross-slabs, two are decorated with triskeles, one with a maze pattern and a fragment of one with an inscription. Six of these slabs are now in the NMI. The remainder, apart from one which is concealed in the graveyard, are in the care of Sligo County Council, some being on display in Sligo Museum. Replicas of twelve of them have been erected against the S wall of the old graveyard and there is a duplicate copy of one on top of the wall. The following description is based on Wallace and Timoney (ibid.) and the numbers assigned to the slabs in that publication have been retained.

This is the original location of a cross-slab that is now in the care of Sligo County Council (see SL014-284003- for present location).
Slab 5: a rectangular slab (0.54m x 0.4m; T 0.05m) with a cross in saltire position. Two lines frame two sides of the design, the remaining sides are open. 

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Revised by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, at the foot of a S-facing slope; in the centre of Knockmore graveyard (SL044-003003-). All that remains of Knockmore Abbey is the ruin of a rectangular church (ext. 25.6m E-W; 8.65m N-S) built of uncoursed mortared stonework. Only a stump at the NE corner, the internal face of the S wall and a short return of the W wall, survive, and much of the E and S walls have recently been rebuilt as a drystone wall. The NE stump contains the N side of the central E window; this has a limestone jamb with chamfered edges. Near the E end of the S wall is a square recess (D 0.6m; H c. 0.8m) with a rounded arch and a ribbed band on both jambs. The base of the recess is covered by rubble but it is probably a piscina (M. A. Timoney 1997, 3). There is a much-ruined doorway near the W end of this wall. Just inside the boundary of the graveyard and NE of the church are two pieces of a window mullion, reused as grave-markers. These match the surviving side of the E window; one is decorated on its internal face with a simple knot motif. A drawing from the 1830s shows this window with three mullions rising to four round sub-arches with tracery overhead (OSNB vol. 1, 435). The interior of the church contains many 19th- and 20th-century burials. Knockmore Abbey was established for the Carmelites c. 1320 (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 290; M. A. Timoney 1997); according to Cowell (1997, 147), it was founded by Edmund O'Gara of Moygara Castle (SL044-052001-). The surviving architectural features, though very fragmentary, appear to be 15th century in date. Four cross-slabs (SL044-003002-; SL044-003004-; SL044-003005-; SL044-003006-) were found loose within and to the W of the friary in the 1970s and 1980s but only one of these can be located. 'Tobernambraher' holy well (SL044-004----) is c. 160m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of the ESE end of a ridge and 15m W of another rath (SL044-006003-). A raised roughly circular area (33.6m E-W; 34m N-S) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.2m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.45m) with a slight internal lip NW-E and elsewhere by a scarp. An external fosse is evident NW-N as a shallow depression (Wth 2.5m; ext. D 0.3m) marked by rushes and irises and N-NE by rushes and irises only. The interior slopes slightly down to S and there is a possible souterrain (SL044-006002-) in the W half. There is a low slumped section (Wth 2-2.5m) in the scarp at S, now blocked by the post and wire fence that tops the perimeter NE-W. Breaks also occur at ESE (Wth 1.5m) and at WSW (Wth 1.4m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a N-facing slope. The well utilised a natural spring emerging at the base of the slope. It has been converted into a county council reservoir and is enclosed by a rectangular concrete shed (11m E-W; 8.5m N-S). No structural remains of the holy well survive. In 1836 it was recorded that the well was known as 'Tobar na Naomh' with a traditional Patron Day on 15th August (OSL, 229). A holy well (SL044-081----) named 'Tober-na-neeve or the Well of the Saints' is recorded in Carrowntemple, c. 2.5km to SW, and had its patron day on 15th August. A penitential cairn (SL044-047002-) and a cross-slab (SL044-047003-) lie c. 9m to ESE and there is a burnt spread (SL044-047006-) at the NW corner of the shed. A cashel (SL044-048001-) is located at the top of the slope to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a N-facing slope and 9m ESE of a holy well (SL044-047001-). A roughly circular cairn (4m N-S; 3.6m E-W; H 1.4m) of stones and slabs with a slightly domed profile, partially obscured by sod and brambles. In places glimpses of coursed stonework are evident. Projecting slightly from the W side is a roughly coursed drystone facade (H 0.5m) of horizontally laid slabs with a flat top (0.5m E-W; 0.6m N-S). The cairn rises gently for c. 0.5m behind the top of the facade. Propped up on the flat top of the facade at W is a cross-slab (SL044-047003-). A large upright slab (H 0.65m; Wth 0.8m E-W; T c. 0.12m) is embedded in the ground at the base of the N side of the cairn. There is a small circular perforation (diam. 0.005m) close to the top edge on the E side of the slab. A cashel (SL044-048001-) is located at the top of the slope to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the base of a N-facing slope and on top of the W side of a penitential cairn (SL044-047002-). A lozenge-shaped sandstone slab (0.5m x 0.48m; T 0.01m) incised on one face with a triple-lined, equal-armed cross, enclosed in a double incised circle (ext. diam. 0.29m). The arms of the cross appear to extend to the edge of the outer circle. A tiny indentation or cupmark is picked out in the centre of each quadrant of the circle. The central incised line at the top of the cross shaft continues beyond the circle to form the shaft of a small single-line cross enclosed within a circle (diam. 0.12m) intersecting with the outer ring of the double circle. The small cross and circle appear to be executed somewhat more simply than the larger cross. There is a holy well (SL044-047001-) c. 9m to WNW and a cashel (SL044-048001-) at the top of the slope to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on level ground at the top of a N-facing slope overlooking a low-lying expanse of damp pasture. A spring at the base of the slope to S is the location for a holy well (SL044-047001-) adjacent to which is a leacht cuimhne (SL044-04702-) with a cross-slab (SL044-047003-). A slightly raised oval area (54.5m E-W; 41.4m N-S) enclosed by a ruined stone wall (Wth 4-4.5m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 1.2m). The wall is especially low and poorly preserved NE-SE. Stones protrude randomly from the sod cover but a few large stones visible in places N-NE may be the remains of stone facing. Loose field-clearance stones and boulders are heaped on top of the wall around its circuit. There is a large break (Wth 6m) in the wall at WNW. The interior is slightly elevated in the NE quadrant with a very slight slope from there down to SE and SW. At S the outer edge of the wall is incorporated into a substantial roughly coursed drystone field wall (Wth 2.2m; H 1.8) on an E-W axis. Where the field wall intersects (L c. 10m) with the cashel, it is constructed of larger stones than elsewhere along its length. A possible limekiln (SL044-048002-) is built into the external face of the cashel wall at N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Near the S end of a ridge overlooking low-lying ground; in the centre of Carrowntemple graveyard (SL044-056002-) and within an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL044-056006-). All that remains standing of the church is its SE corner (ext. c. 6.3m E-W; c. 1.8m N-S; H c. 3m; wall T c. 0.65m). This is built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar, and is now heavily encased by ivy. The only evident feature is the splayed side of the E window, where the E wall now breaks off. The interior is filled with grave-plots, marked by low uninscribed stones and by 20th-century headstones. Probably the remains of the medieval parish church of Kilfree (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 363-4). Thirteen cross-slabs (SL044-056004-) and a slab rough-out were found in the graveyard, mainly to the E and S of the church.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the centre of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL044-056006-), on the N side of a road. A roughly rectangular graveyard (c. 30m N-S; c. 25m E-W) enclosed by a field boundary on the W side and by the remnants of a boundary wall on the N side; the E and S sides are defined by a stone-faced scarped edge overlooking a 1960s extension. The entrance gate is at the W end of the S side. The interior is mostly under grass but the N end is densely covered by scrub. The graveyard contains many 19th- and 20th-century graves and lines of low uninscribed grave-markers. Fragments of a quernstone (diam. c. 0.35m) lie in the SE corner. In the centre are the fragmentary remains of the medieval parish church of Kilfree (SL044-056001-). Thirteen cross-slabs (SL044-056004-) and a slab rough-out were found in various locations in the graveyard. Replicas of 12 of the cross-slabs have been erected along the stone-faced scarp on the S side. Fragments of quernstones, metal slag and a hammer stone which were found in the graveyard are in the NMI (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). There is a souterrain (SL044-056003-) c. 20m to the NW and a second souterrain (SL044-056007-) c. 150m to the W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In Carrowntemple ecclesiastical enclosure (SL044-056006-). Two parallel and adjacent drystone-built chambers were described by Wallace and Timoney (1987, 45-6) within the ecclesiastical enclosure and c. 20m NW of the graveyard (SL044-056002-). Both chambers contained a considerable amount of fill and it was not possible to determine if they were connected. Sandstone was used for the walls and roof lintels in both chambers. A small opening, covered by a flat circular stone (diam. 0.4m; T 0.05m), led into one chamber (3.2m x 1.55m) which had an air-vent in its SW corner and an entrance on its N side. The second chamber (3.15m x 1.35m; H 1.45m) had a single course of corbelling supporting the roof lintels, one of which was broken. A possible roof lintel which was also noted a short distance to the NE and at right angles to the chambers may represent a further chamber. Recorded in 1836 as a 'cave or rather covered passage' (OSNB vol. 1, 417). These chambers are no longer accessible (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). A second souterrain (SL044-056007-) lies c. 130m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Thirteen Early Christian slabs and a slab rough-out were found in various locations around Carrowntemple graveyard (SL044-056002-), mainly to the S and E of the church (SL044-056001-), and were described by Wallace and Timoney (1987, 43-61). The remainder, apart from one which is concealed in the graveyard, are in the care of Sligo County Council, some being on display in Sligo Museum. Replicas of twelve of them have been erected against the S wall of the old graveyard and there is a duplicate copy of one on top of the wall. The following description is based on Wallace and Timoney (ibid.) and the numbers assigned to the slabs in that publication have been retained.

Slab 10: a roughly rectangular slab (1.21m x 0.47m; T 0.06-0.10m) with a rounded top and a tenon at the base. Both faces are decorated. The smooth slab face features a human figure which comprises a face enclosed by an outer circle, a short naked body with long arms and short legs with relatively large feet. The other face has a cross with a fret pattern below it. The cross comprises a pair of triple-strand ribbons crossed at right-angles and knotted at their extremities. The design below the cross has flaked off leaving only the vestiges of a rectilinear or fret pattern on the upper section. A plinth stone (diam. 0.75m; T 0.19m) with a subrectangular mortise-hole (26.5 cm x 10.5cm) probably held this double-sided slab (Timoney 2002a, 142). This slab is in the National Museum of Ireland (DU018-231----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Revised by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In the water outside the W edge of a drumlin, in a visually strategic position near the outflow of Lough Gara into the Boyle River. Most of the view is cut off by the surrounding drumlins but mountain tops such as the Curlews and Mullaghtee can be seen in the distance. A drop-shaped low-cairn crannog (19.7m N-S; 13.4m E-W; H 1.16m above the lake-bed) with an even surface of gravel and small subangular stones (diam. 0.05-0.1m) as well as a loose scatter of limestone boulders. The majority of the stones are well-set into the ground and the island is, to a large extent, probably natural, perhaps built by cutting off the tip of the drumlin with a channel a few metres wide. Two causeways are connected to it: one (8.3m E-W) connects with the shore to the E and consists of subangular stones (c. 0.3-0.4m) packed in at least two layers; the other (7.6m N-S; 1.4m E-W) which leads out in a NNW direction to a large boulder (1.7m x 1.1m) in the water is more neatly built, appears more stable and consists of smaller stones. The edge of the crannog is partially submerged and slopes down gradually. The crannog has a sparse cover of grass and a few bushes. A lacustrine enclosure (SL045-016----) is c. 200m to N. A crannog (SL045-009----) is c. 250m to ENE. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 002)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a dry meadow, at the stony N shore of the outflow of Lough Gara into the Boyle River. Two stone arm-like features, c. 8m apart, define the S portion of a slightly sunken oval area (23.5m N-S; 41m E-W). The E arm is an irregular to kidney-shaped island (20m N-S; 13.5m E-W; H 0.6m) with an uneven surface. In the gap between the 'arms' is an irregular concentration of stones (diam. c. 5m). The SE arm (31.8m E-W; 18m N-S) consists of stones well set into the ground and surrounded by soil that merges into the meadow to N. Two crannogs (SL045-008----; SL045-009----) are c. 200m to S and c. 250m to SE respectively. A moated site (SL045-007002-) lies c. 40m to N. (Fredengren 2002, KILA H1)

source_data.original_text:
In a secluded bay, on the E shore of Lough Gara, exposed during summer and submerged in winter. The shoreline is stony while the lake-bed is marly. A large crannog (SL047-017----) is visible c. 100m to E. A low-cairn crannog (6m N-S; 7.5m E-W; H 0.9m) consisting of a floor of shattered angular stones spread out on an elevation of marl. There are about 14 subangular stones (diam. 0.3-0.4m) outside the edge N-ESE. The site is distinct in edge and height W-E while it blends into the shoreline to the S. Wood from piles along the edge of crannog has been dated to the later early medieval period (Fredengren 2002, KILA 011). The site is grass-covered and surrounded by reeds. It is one of three crannogs (SL047-017----; SL047-018005-) and amongst a group of six possible crannogs (SL047-015----; SL047-018001-; SL047-018002-; SL047-018003-; SL047-018004-; SL047-018006-) in this bay. (Cross 1953, fig. 1)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow, on the shore of Lough Gara in a secluded bay, surrounded by drumlins. The top of the crannog is very overgrown with shrubs and trees, while the edges are clearer. This is a high-cairn crannog (21.1m N-S; 18.4m E-W; max. H 2.49m above the meadow), the surface of which consists of loosely packed subangular stones (diam. c. 0.4m) on top of shattered fire-cracked stones mixed with animal bones. The eastern (landward) edge drops distinctly to the water meadow while the W edge slopes gradually down towards open water. The E portion is grass-covered with very few stones exposed, while the S portion consists of a denser concentration of loose stones. A grass-covered mid-cairn or plateau (6m N-S, 5.6m E-W) lies to the SE of the centre, surrounded by a plateau that is more pronounced at S (Wth 3.5m) while barely discernible at E. To N is a ramp that seems to lead from the N part of the berm up to the plateau in a W direction. The berm has a somewhat irregular form. The plateau is wider towards the lake. One of a group of six possible crannogs (SL047-016----; SL047-018001-; SL047-018002-; SL047-018003-; SL047-018004-; SL047-018006-) and three crannogs (SL047-015----; SL047-018005-) in this bay. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 009)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 212/1955).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure' and 'Ringfort (Rath/Cashel)' respectively. Indicated on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map as a roughly circular depression (diam. c. 30m). In undulating pasture. When inspected in 2000 it was recorded that this is now evident as a square quarried out area (c. 26m N-S; c. 28m E-W). The N end of the W side, the N side and the E side of this sunken feature are dug directly into the natural slope producing high almost vertical inward facing scarps. The N side has the highest scarp (H 2.5-3m) while the lowest is at the S (H c. 1m). It serves as a sump for waste water from the house/farm situated up-slope to N. There is no evidence that this an archaeological monument. The remains of a rath (SL047-034----) lies a short distance to the SE.  


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the E side of a road and adjacent to the Sligo-Roscommon border. A raised square area (31m N-S; 31m E-W) enclosed by two earthen banks with intervening and external fosses. The inner bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.1m) is flat-topped with a low internal rim and a steep-sided external slope. The outer bank (Wth 7.1m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.6m) is flat-topped and broad based with steeply sloping sides and is substantial on the E and S sides. A section of the outer bank (L 14m) at the S end of the W side is levelled. The intervening fosse (Wth 2.6m) is flat-bottomed and steep-sided. The external fosse (Wth 2.5m; D 0.35m) is evident as a shallow depression on the E and S sides and is almost entirely silted-up elsewhere. The entrance is at the E end of the N side with gaps in the inner and outer banks (Wth 2m and 1.8m respectively) and a causeway (Wth 2.5m) across the fosse. A single large stone flanks the W side of the causeway. Immediately E of the entrance, the inner face of the external bank has a distinctive slump (Wth c. 2m; L c. 4-5m). The interior is level and grass-covered. There is a low sod-covered rise (c. 9.5m N-S; c. 3.6m E-W; H 0.3m) in the centre, with a line of closely set stones (L 2m) at the N end of the E side and possibly also on the W side. A relict field boundary extends for c. 55m from the SW corner of the moated site. Appended to the S side of this boundary, at its junction with the moated site, is a roughly triangular earthen platform (7.3m N-S; 16m E-W; H 0.55m). The garden of a recently constructed bungalow is 16m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In poorly drained level pasture, at the W end of a low natural elevation in a narrow valley. A slightly raised roughly circular area (c. 23m N-S; 27.6m E-W) defined by a scarp, an outer bank and an intervening and external fosse. All enclosing elements are levelled NW-NE and the area is marked by a dense growth of rushes. The scarp (H 0.9m) is generally well defined NE-NW. The intervening flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 3.2m) is marked by a growth of rushes NE-NW; elsewhere the fosse is evident as band of wet ground. The outer bank (Wth 5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.1m) is partially truncated NE-E by a substantial field boundary with a drain but elsewhere it is broad with a compact rounded profile, flattened on the top in places. The external fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.2m) is evident ESE-NW as narrow shallow depression, indicated mainly by a growth of rushes, and truncated NE-E by a field boundary. There is an entrance at E consisting of a causeway (Wth 3.2m) across the intervening fosse with traces of a corresponding gap in the outer bank. The W half of the interior is higher than the E half with a gradual slope down towards centre. There is a stream c. 15m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In poorly drained pasture, at the bottom of a valley. A raised circular area (40.8m N-S; 37m E-W) defined by the remains of an earthen bank (Wth c. 2m; int. H 0.35m; ext. H 2.35m) along the S arc and elsewhere by a scarp (H 2.5m). A broad flat-bottomed intervening fosse (Wth 3.8m at base) is evident all round, the S arc is waterlogged. There is a broad steep-sided outer bank (Wth 7m; int. H 1.75m; ext. H 1.5m) with a flattened top which, where eroded, reveals a stony core. It is incorporated into a field boundary NE-E. There is a drain (Wth 1m) immediately outside the outer bank SSE-SW. The entrance at SE consists of a gap (Wth 3m) in the inner bank, a causeway (Wth c. 4m) across the fosse and a corresponding gap in the outer bank which is now blocked by a field boundary. There is a small irregular cairn (3.5m N-S; 3.3m E-W; H 0.6m) of moss-covered stones to W of centre of the level interior. The banks are overgrown with bushes and the fosse is blocked in places by fallen trees.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on a gentle slope towards the W end of, and occupying almost the full width of, a narrow ridge. In a grassy verge, on the W side of the Frenchpark-Boyle road and adjacent to the E side of a field boundary. The well, which is slightly sunken below the road level, is enclosed in a dilapidated concrete structure (int. dims. 1.1m E-W; 1.05m N-S). The entrance is in the centre of the S wall. Access to the well is through a small concrete annexe immediately to the front into which steps lead down from ground level. There is no evidence of recent veneration at this well. In 1836 it was recorded that the 'patron-day is the 11th of August, St. Araght's (Athracht's) Day, on which stations used to be performed' (OSL, 233). The site of a nunnery (SL047-083001-) and a graveyard (SL047-083002-) are c. 600m to N.

raw_items.raw_text: Donn Óg Mac Airechtaigh and his small band of men laid in wait for the army of Richard de Burgh in 1230

source_data.original_text:
Located at the highest point on a plateau of rough bog on the W side of the Curlew Mountains, c. 400m from the border with Co. Roscommon. The expanse of bog is bordered at NW, NE and SE by forestry plantations. The location provides extensive views, with Brislagh Hill prominent to E, Keshcorran Mountain with its passge tomb cairn (SL040-008----) on the skyline to NNW, and one of the Carrowkeel passage tombs (SL040-096----) visible in the Bricklieve Mountains to NNE. This cairn is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps, however, the location is indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map as a trigonometrical station. Roughly circular cairn (diam. c. 12m; H c. 0.6m) composed of rounded sandstone blocks (size range c. 0.2-0.4m). The perimeter of the cairn is partly concealed by an overlying layer of peat. The cairn has suffered disturbance: in the centre is circular pile or platform of stones (diam. 2.8m; H 1.5m) which appears to have been a built using cairn stones to serve as a trigonometrical station. Encircling it at a distance of c. 1.8m is a roughly built drystone wall (Wth 0.5m; H 0.6m) which encloses a space of diameter c. 5m. This drystone wall is located c. 2.5m in from the outer edge of the cairn. The cairn may be the ‘Finn-Charn’, mentioned in the Annals of Connacht and the Annals of Loch Cé, close to which Donn Óg Mac Airechtaigh and his small band of men laid in wait for the army of Richard de Burgh in 1230. During the ensuing battle, Donn Óg died fighting with his axe, having suffered many wounds and been pierced by five arrows (AC 1230.4; ALC 1230.7-110) (pers. comm. Sam Moore and Lydia Harris, Sligo IT. June 2015).

Attached image uploaded courtesy of Sam Moore and Lydia Harris, Sligo IT:

SL045-023----_0.1.JPG cairn viewed from SW, with ranging rods indicating approximate extent of cairn. 

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 12 June 2015

The following account of its discovery is recorded by Timoney (2008-9): ‘In April 2007, on a visit to Killaraght graveyard. Co. Sligo, to check an 18th century headstone the author discovered an Early Christian cross slab which had been reused as a grave memorial in recent times. The Old Red Sandstone slab was lying on the ground in front of the Goldrick family grave plot in the old section of the graveyard. The slab measures 99cm long, the upper two thirds is about 40cm in width with a maximum thickness of 8.5cm. The left side of the slab is complete but parts of the right side have been cut or broken off. The inscribed cross with T-shaped terminals measures 14.5cm long and 21cm wide. In poorly drained rush-covered grazing, on top of a narrow ridge. A slightly raised circular area (6.7m N-S; 6.6m E-W) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.5m) has a low internal face. The fosse (Wth 2m) is shallow and flat-bottomed and marginally raised above exterior ground level. The outer bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident as a low compact rise with a well-defined external face. The overall diameter is 15m N-S and 15.5m E-W and it is almost completely engulfed in rushes. A ring-barrow (SL047-071----) lies c. 55m to E. This ring-barrow is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

source_data.original_text:
Listed in the RMP (1994) an classified as 'Enclosure'. Not marked on the 1838 edition of the OS 6" map. Depicted a small wedge-shaped field on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map. On a natural terrace of dry ground, in otherwise waterlogged pasture. Upon inspection in 2000 the visible remains comprised a roughly triangular area (28.5m WNW-ESE; c. 39m NNE-SSW) defined by a flat-topped earthen bank (Wth 2.2m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 1.1.2m) with an external flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 2m; ext. D 0.4m) on the NNW and SW sides and by a linear field boundary (Wth 2m; int. H 0.75m; ext. H 1.5m) with a substantial external drain, along the E side. There is a break (Wth c. 10m) at the NE end of the NNW side which allows cattle access to interior. Remnants of a counterscarp bank (Wth 1.5m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.3m) are evident outside the fosse on the SW side. The interior is raised c. 0.8m above the external ground level on the NNW and SW sides. The field boundary extends beyond the enclosure to SSW while at the NNE end it intersects with another field boundary. It was concluded that this is a natural terrace which has been transformed, probably in recent times, into a roughly triangular field. It is likely to be post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 06 December 2011

Listed in both the SMR (1989) and the RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure'.  In waterlogged pasture, immediately N of a triangular field (SL047-073001-). Inspection in 2000 revealed that this is a low, naturally-occurring elevation with sides that slope gently down to the E and SE. This area is now enclosed by field boundaries creating a roughly square field (c. 34.5m E-W; 33m N-S) with linear N and E sides and gently curved S and W sides. The interior slopes gently down to NW. The W half of the field is planted with conifers while much of the E half is occupied by a corrugated iron barn and a small concrete enclosure and cattle crush. It was concluded that there are no upstanding remains visible to suggest that this is an archaeological monument.

In the SE quadrant of a moated site (SL045-007002-). According to local tradition, a low irregular platform (c. 11m NE-SW; 8.5m NW-SE; H 0.8m) on the S side of the moated site, is the remains of an O'Gara castle. Though now sod-covered, the platform appears to be largely composed of stones. Remnants of a rough stone facing are evident at NNE and E, whilst elsewhere stones protrude randomly from the surface. Incorporated into the SW corner of the platform are remnants of a circular stone-lined feature (diam. 2m; H 0.6m), probably the remains of a limekiln.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). source_data.original_text:
In low-lying wet pasture, on the S side of a road and c. 80m W of Cuppanagh Bridge over the River Boyle. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a circular enclosure (int. diam. c. 20m) close to the shore of Lough Gara. A densely overgrown slightly raised subrectangular area (c. 30m NNE-SSW; c. 40m ENE-WSW), the N side of which is mostly truncated by the road. The E and S sides are defined by a scarp (H c. 0.6m), degraded and marked only by a loose scattering of stones in places especially on the S side. The W side is defined by a stony bank (Wth 4.6m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.4m) and a wet external flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 4.8m; D 1m), mostly choked by rushes. The N end of the fosse curves around to the E for c. 10m. The outer edge of the fosse is topped by the remnants of a field boundary wall and a line of bushes. Both the bank and fosse show evidence of recent modification. The interior is generally level but a platform in the SE quadrant is possibly the remains of a castle (SL045-007001-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, in Killaraght graveyard (SL047-083002-) and within a field system (SL047-083004-). Probably the site of a convent founded by St Attracta which, according to tradition, was built by St Patrick (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 320-21). A nunnery and hospital (SL047-083007-) existed here into the 16th century and an abbess of Killaraght is mentioned in 1591 (ibid.). A 'house of nuns of Killaraght' still stood here in the 1680s (Ó Muraíle 2002, 242, n. 48). It is also probably the site of the medieval parish church of Killaraght. According to local tradition, there was a church ruin in the NW quadrant of the graveyard. Several blocks of dressed stone, found during a graveyard clean up, are the only recent indication of a church here (Mount 1994a). A road (SL047-083003-) lies c. 200m to the NE. 'Toberaraght' holy well (SL047-081----) is c. 600m to the S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating stony pasture. A system of roughly rectangular fields indicated only on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. The boundaries of these are mainly earthen with a few of earth and stone. They are of fairly uniform dimensions (Wth 1.7-2m; H 0.5m) but vary greatly in degree of preservation. Killaraght graveyard (SL047-083002-) and the site of a church (SL047-08301-) are roughly in the centre of the field system. Immediately to SW of the graveyard is a faint pattern of two or three small fields (c. 14m E-W; c. 28m N-S) which are not indicated on any OS 6-inch map. An even more faint outline of a similar field pattern is evident to SE. A moated site (SL047-083008-) lies c. 50m W of the graveyard. The relict field system is now overlain by a grid pattern of N-S and E-W field boundaries. There is a mound barrow (SL047-083005-) c. 150m SW of the graveyard and another (SL047-083006-) c. 170m to NE, both also within the field system. In the same townland is a second field system (SL047-084003-) c. 300m to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In rough grazing, on top of a low ridge. A raised circular area (19.8m N-S; 20m E-W) defined by a scarp with an intervening fosse and an outer bank. The scarp (H 1.2m) has an almost vertical face and retains a slight internal lip (Wth 2m) S-SW. The outer bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.4m) is evident NE-SSW, incorporated into or replaced by a linear field boundary at W and truncated by another field boundary at N. The intervening fosse (Wth 3.3m) is also evident NE-SSW, elsewhere it is distinguished by a band of wet ground densely covered with rushes. A section of a linear bank (L 14m; Wth 2.3m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.55m) evident ENE-ESE, 2.3m outside the external bank may be the remains of a second bank but could also be a remnant of a field boundary. The interior slopes slightly down from the centre to N. A slump (Wth 1.4m) in the scarp at ESE is directly opposite a break (Wth 3.5m) in the outer bank. A field system (SL047-084003-) lies c. 20m N and downslope of the rath and an enclosure (SL047-084002-) lies c. 30m to E. There is a burnt mound (SL047-084004-) c. 100m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the margins of a flat expanse of marshy pasture, overlooked by rising ground to S. The moated site is low and degraded and barely visible amidst the surrounding rushes. A low square platform (c. 21m NW-SE; 22m NE-SW), with rounded corners, defined by a scarp (H 0.6m) with an intervening fosse (Wth 3m at NE; 4.8m at SW) and an external bank (Wth 3-3.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.4m). The platform is level and covered with rushes. The enclosing elements are best preserved on the SW side and less well preserved, but still visible, on the NW and NE sides. A grassy cropmark (Wth c. 2m) on top of the scarp at the W end of the SW side and on the NW side may indicate a levelled inner bank. The fosse is marked by a dense growth of rushes and is narrower on the NE side. The outer bank appears as a low grassy rise, degraded in parts on the NW and NE sides to little more than a grassy cropmark. On the E corner, the SE side and the S corner the scarp is very poorly defined, the fosse cannot be distinguished from the surrounding expanse of wet ground and the outer bank is not evident. The site is crossed NE of centre by a field boundary and drain on a NW-SE axis. A strip of flat wet ground (Wth 12m) separates the moated site from the gently rising dry ground to S. This area is crossed by a stony causeway (Wth 2.3m) that cuts through the outer bank on the SW side and continues over the fosse to the platform. The causeway continues across the platform, cutting the field boundary, the fosse and the outer bank on the NE side.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of a narrow ridge with good views. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a roughly circular enclosure and on the 1942-3 OS 6-inch map as a subrectangular enclosure. A level subrectangular area (32.7m WNW-ESE; 25m NNE-SSW) raised c. 0.8m above the surrounding ground level and enclosed by linear field boundaries topped with ash and hawthorn trees and brambles. The enclosing boundaries (Wth 2-2.4m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 1.2m) have a vertical external face, with traces of external stone facing evident on the N side. The N, E and S sides are straight but the W side retains a slight curve, particularly at the NW corner. Outside the bank at the E end of the S side there is a broad band (Wth c. 6m) of damp ground marked by a dense growth of rushes, possibly indicating an infilled fosse. A 'corn kiln', indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map on the line of the field boundary to NNE was not located. An abandoned farmstead lies c. 30m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On the SE-facing spine of a narrow-topped ridge. A raised circular area (int. diam. 31m E-W; 31m N-S) enclosed by three earthen banks, best preserved along the W and S arcs, with intervening fosses. The inner bank is the highest (Wth 2.85m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 0.8m) and has possible stone facing. The middle bank (Wth 1.9m; ext. H 0.45m) drops 0.4m to base of inner fosse. The external bank (Wth 2.8m; ext. H 0.6m) drops 0.6m to the base of the middle fosse. There are narrow gaps through the inner, middle and outer banks (Wth 1m, 1.4m and 1m respectively) at W. The inner and middle fosses (Wth 1.95m and Wth 2.2m respectively) are both waterlogged. The interior rises towards the centre and slopes down towards E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On top of a broad flat-topped knoll, overlooking the Owenmore River c. 100m to S. The NW half of this rath has been quarried away. The remains consist of a substantially raised D-shaped platform (dims. 16m NNW-SSE) defined on the straight NW side (L 23.5m ENE-WSW) by a quarry and NE-WSW by a high curving scarp (H 2.7m) with external fosse (Wth c. 8.5m; D 1.9m). The curving scarp is engulfed in hawthorn and blackthorn bushes and brambles. The fosse survives N-E as a shallow depression (Wth 4.7m; D 0.6m) but E-SW it is broad, flat-bottomed and dug deeply into the top of the knoll close to break of slope so that immediately outside the fosse the ground falls away in a steep natural slope. The outer edge of the fosse E-S is engulfed in brambles and thorn bushes. The straight side of the platform consists of an irregular, slumped, grass-covered scarp (H 1.55m) the result of quarrying. A curving undulation is evident NNW-NNE, 18m to NNW of the quarry scarp, and may indicate the line of the fosse on this side. The intervening quarried space, between this undulation and the remains of the interior, is slightly sunken and has an uneven surface.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a low ridge. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 38m). The remains consist of a slightly raised D-shaped area (dims. 42m N-S; 34m E-W) defined WSW-NE by a gapped earthen bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.2m) truncated at E by a concrete shed. A slight undulation at SW probably indicates another portion of the bank which has been levelled. The straight S side is bordered by a vertical S-facing scarp (H 1m) revetted with concrete walling, immediately to S of which is a house. Outside the bank WSW-NW, and respecting its curve, is an earth and stone field boundary (Wth 1.5m). The intervening space (Wth 4m) is c. 0.6m below both the rath interior and ground level in the field to W and may indicate a fosse. A slight depression (Wth 3.5m) outside the bank at NNW may also be evidence of an external fosse. There are several narrow eroded breaks in the bank and at NE a larger slumped gap (Wth 2.5m). Within the level interior, adjacent to bank at N, is a slight dip in ground level corresponding with a very low flat-topped rectangular rise (c. 6m E-W; 4m N-S) immediately outside the bank. These features probably indicate the site of a small rectangular structure shown straddling the bank on the 1942-3 OS 6-inch map. There is a water trough in the interior. In 1836 three 'old forts' (see SL044-080---- and SL044-019----) were recorded in the townland of Greyfield (OSNB vol. 1, 423).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low drumlin at break of slope on the W side where the ground slopes down to a stream. Indicated as a circular enclosure on the 1942-3 OS 6-inch map. A subrectangular area (25.4m N-S; 22.4m E-W) with rounded corners, defined on the N, E and S sides by a flat-topped stony bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.4m) with traces of stone kerbing. A scarp (H 1.7m), coinciding with the natural break of slope, defines the interior along the W side and at the SW and NW corners. The scarp at the SW corner is topped by a slight stony rim. The bank is sod-covered, poorly preserved and to NW and W largely obscured by brambles, hawthorn bushes and heaps of loose stones. The stone kerbing is most clearly seen at the SE corner and along the E half of the S side but elsewhere is indicated only by an occasional stone. There is a break (Wth 5m) in the bank in the middle of the N side and another (Wth 3.4m) towards the W end of the S side. The scarp appears rather uneven and irregular with occasional stones and boulders protruding randomly from the long grass cover. The interior is level, grassy and featureless.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, at the NW end of a peninsula jutting westwards into the S part of Lough Gara.
According to local information, this is the location of a monastery or convent (pers. comm. Kevin Forde 2020). The remains consist of a low, grass-covered earth and stone bank (Wth 2.5m; H 0.3-0.6m) which curves E−WNW in a shallow arc (cord L 20m). The arc of bank spans the space between two straight, roughly N−S field boundaries/hedgerows, which clip the terminals of the arc. A low concentration (diam. c. 2m) of stones protrudes from the grass close to the E terminal. The space enclosed by the arc consists of rough, uneven ground, which stretches N for c. 22m to an E−W scarp/hedgerow defining the N edge of the field. The E−W scarp drops c. 0.6m to a flat expanse of damp ground, which stretches 35-40m N to the lake shore and is likely to have been at least partly inundated in the past when lake levels were higher.
There is a local tradition of buildings in the vicinity of the arc of bank but none are now visible; the area is covered in long grass, rushes and clumps of brambles.
There are no known documentary sources to corroborate the existence of a religious foundation here; it is not listed in A. Gwynn and R.N. Hadcock, 'Medieval Religious Houses. Ireland' (1970). The nature and date of this site remain uncertain.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 21 May 2021

In pasture, straddling a break of slope at the top of the S-facing slope of an E-W ridge. It is not shown on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map but is indicated on the 1942-3 edition by a shallow arc of hachures E-SSW, in the NW corner of a field. A roughly square area (33.7m N-S; c. 30m E-W) bordered on the S side by a high S-facing scarp (H c. 2m) cut into the ridge slope, and on W and N sides by straight field boundaries. On the E side there are no evident remains of an enclosing element. The scarp is mostly straight but curves slightly at the SE corner where it has been partially dug away. The scarp and field boundaries are engulfed in brambles and thorn bushes. The interior slopes gently down to S following the ridge slope. There is a possibility that this may be the remains of an enclosure but the surviving remains and the map evidence are not sufficient to warrant classifying it as such.

In pasture, on a N-facing slope and just below the summit of a ridge. A roughly circular area (32m E-W; 28m N-S) defined NW-E by a scarp (H 1.45m) with a slight internal lip (Wth c. 2m), ESE-S by a field boundary wall (Wth 0.7m; H 0.8m) and SSW-W by an earthen bank (Wth c. 4m; int. Abutting the outer edge of the fosse at NW is a low triangular flat-topped rise (4m NE-SW; 4m NW-SE; H 0.5m). The bank and fosse at S are quite densely covered in brambles and bushes. Occasional sycamores and ash trees grow elsewhere around the perimeter.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, straddling a break of slope at the NE end of a drumlin ridge overlooking a damp, boggy valley. A raised roughly circular area (diam. 43.2m x 40.4m) enclosed by a substantial earthen bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1.9m) with a pronounced external face but a rather dilapidated and slumped internal face. The bank is primarily earthen but stones protrude randomly in places. A rough external facing of stone evident N-NE is the result of the incorporation of the bank into a field boundary. The bank is thickly ringed with hazel, blackthorn and brambles. A depression (Wth c. 4m) outside the bank W-NW is defined by a gentle natural rise in ground level and may indicate an external fosse. Outside the bank to E there appears to be a slight terrace (Wth c. 4m) but it is difficult to trace due to dense overgrowth. The W half of the interior is slightly higher than the E half with a slight slope down from the centre to N, E and SE, levelling out 4-6m from the inner face of the bank. This reflects the natural slope of the ridge and gives the effect of a shallow fosse-like depression just inside the bank N-SE. The interior is grassy and relatively clear of overgrowth. There are badger sets in the S half of the interior. Another rath (SL044-049----) lies c. 50m to WNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Almost 1km W of the N end of Lough Gara on a patch of rocky pasture in gently rolling land. The remains of a court (min. L 6m; Wth c. 8m at its inner end) at the NW, its more westerly arm represented by four stones and the opposite arm by two, opens into two galleries set side by side. Little remains of the more westerly gallery (min. L 7m) the entrance to which is formed by two jambs. A sidestone abuts the more easterly of these and there is another on the same side almost 4m to the S. Opposite this there is another sidestone and between them what appears to be a segmenting jamb. Its presence indicates there was further gallery structure here. The second gallery (min. L 6.5m) consists of an antechamber represented by the more easterly entrance jamb and a sidestone abutting it. Segmenting jambs separate this from a chamber the E side of which is represented by a single stone and the W side by two stones. Another pair of segmenting jambs stand between the last and another chamber, its intact W side of two stones and two of a likely original three stones in place at the E. A segmenting jamb adjoins the outer end of the W side of this indicating that there was at least one further chamber here. There are some displaced stones at the site. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 79-80, no. 126)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

SL044-051----_01.jpg. View of the court from north-west showing the court stones (right) and the two entrance jambs of the western gallery.

See linked document with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989)

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 29 August 2014

source_data.original_text:
Attached to the summer shoreline, in a small lagoon in the NW corner of Lough Gara. A kidney-shaped low-cairn crannog (14m N-S; 14m E-W; H 1.02m above the muddy lake-bed) the surface of which consists of shattered angular stones (diam. 0.03-0.05m) with some larger subangular stones (diam. 0.3-0.4m). The crannog is high in the centre, sloping gradually down towards the edges. Along the water's edge S-SW are c. 13 horizontal roundwood posts. Large horizontal timbers (L 3m; Wth 0.25m) are also evident in the water to E as well as a number of quite substantial flagstones placed on a layer of scattered stones. The crannog edge is distinct in material but not in shape. A few sally trees grow on it. This crannog has been radiocarbon dated to the early medieval period and artifacts associated with it support that date (Fredengren 2002, KILF 005). (Cross 1953, fig. 1).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the break of a NNE-facing slope overlooking a broad expanse of poorly drained pasture. Subrectangular area (int. dims. 17.2m N-S; 21m E-W) enclosed on the N, E and S sides by a drystone wall (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 1.7m) with rounded corners, and bordered on the W side by a NNE-SSW field boundary wall (Wth 1.4m; H 1m). Where it intersects with the enclosure, the field boundary wall is slightly more substantial than elsewhere along its length. The interior is a level terrace cut into the natural slope. Moss and blackthorn bushes obscure much of the wall fabric. The internal wall face is largely reduced to a loose jumble of stones on the N and E sides, and is very dilapidated at S. The external wall face at N and W is also dilapidated and at S is merely a low jumble of moss-covered stones. There is a break (Wth 1m) at the W end of the S wall and another (Wth 0.8m), now blocked by a stone wall, at the W end of the N wall. A small ruined rectangular structure (2.2m N-S; c. 1.8m E-W), with drystone walls, is built into the collapsed inner face of the E wall and clearly post-dates it. A similar roofless rectangular structure (3.6m E-W; 2.3m), with drystone walls (Wth 0.6m; H 1.4m), abuts the external face of the N wall.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a ridge, in the Curlew Mountains. A raised circular area (35m N-S; 35m E-W) enclosed by a ruinous stone wall from which most of the stones have been robbed. A section of wall (Wth 1.2m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 1.3m) with internal and external stone facing and a rubble core, is evident along the S arc and may be original. Elsewhere the cashel wall is replaced by a narrow drystone wall which follows the edge of the raised area in places and elsewhere skirts it internally. The entrance (Wth 0.9m) is at S. The interior is uneven and rises towards the centre.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In a coniferous plantation, on a level area on a NE-facing slope. An exclusion zone of several metres has been left unplanted around the cashel. Indicated on the 1942-3 OS 6-inch map by an arc of hachures SE-SW. A ruined moss-covered stone wall (Wth c. 3m; H 0.5m) survives SE-SW in a shallow arc (C c. 20m). It is engulfed in an impenetrable thicket of blackthorn and brambles and only the SW section could be inspected. This wall may be the remains of a cashel. There is a NW-SE field boundary immediately to N, on the N side of which is a level area (c. 15m E-W) clear of trees which could be the remains of the N half of the cashel.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on a steep NE-facing slope overlooking Lough Gara. A circular area (40.5m NW-SE; 40m NE-SW) enclosed on the upslope SE-WNW by a ruined stone wall and on the downslope by a levelled grassy scarp NW-N and by a stone-faced scarp (H 2m) NNE-SE. The stone wall has an intact external face (H 1.2m) in parts to S and W but is evident mainly as a compact heap of stones (Wth 1.5-2m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.6m). The interior slopes steeply down to NE with the natural hillslope and is covered with long grass and rushes. The perimeter is densely ringed with blackthorn bushes and brambles. The rath has been incorporated into a field system and it is not clear to what extent the extant enclosing wall represents a primary enclosing element or a later modification. A telegraph pole stands on the scarp at N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In a wet meadow, on the NW shore of Lough Gara with views of Moygara castle (SL044-052001-) c. 900m to NW, a cairn (SL044-073----) c. 400m to NE and Mullaghthee in the distance to SW. An oval low-cairn crannog (15m N-S; 20.6m E-W; H 1.07m) with a high soil content. The surface is firm and consists of well-set stones. It is domed and the edges slope gradually down in all directions. There is a mid-cairn in the W portion on which is a vague rectangular outline of stones (5.5m N-S; 2.8m E-W). A row of stones runs parallel to the N edge of this feature. In the water, a short distance to the NE, is a rectangular area (2.7m NE-SW; 1.5m NW-SE) of subangular stones, possibly a small platform crannog or part of a causeway leading out into the water. This is the most southerly of a group of four crannogs (SL044-069----; SL044-070----; SL044-071----). Another crannog (SL044-089----) is c. 150m to SE. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILF 006)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, straddling a natural elevation and overlooking Lough Gara to E. A roughly circular area (28m NNW-SSE) enclosed by a drystone wall (Wth 2m; int. H 2m; ext. H 2.2m) of roughly coursed limestone blocks and slabs. The wall is well preserved SW-N, is reduced internally N-E to a low heap of rubble and externally consists of a facing (H 1.8m) on a scarp cut into the natural slope, some of which has collapsed downslope and topped with a field boundary wall (Wth 0.6m; H 0.5-1m). The wall remains largely intact ESE-SSE but expands in width to 2.4m. From S-SW, where the external ground level is significantly higher than that of the interior, the external wall face is low and almost flush with the external ground level. A trackway (Wth 1.7m) flanked by walls, curves around the cashel SSE-SSW, partially overlying the cashel wall. The only break (Wth c. 2.5m) in the wall is at E and is engulfed in overgrowth. The interior slopes down to NE and E and is largely covered in blackthorn and brambles.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a water-meadow, on the shore at the NW end of Lough Gara. Views are limited in all directions. A high-cairn crannog (c. 22m N-S; 19.2m E-W; H 2.13m above the meadow), the unstable surface of which mainly consists of densely packed sandstone stones. There is a central circular mid-cairn (6m N-S; 6m E-W) with a hollow (c. 1.6m N-S; 2m E-W; D 0.75m) in the surface. There is a distinct drop from the mid-cairn down to the surrounding plateau (Wth 2.5-2.7m) which consists of moss-covered well-sorted stones (diam. 0.2-0.3m) more firmly set in the ground than those of the mid-cairn. The plateau is surrounded by a berm of looser stones. The crannog edge is distinct in material and form. The crannog is densely covered with overgrowth. A small quantity of iron slag was noted between some of the stones during a previous site inspection in 1994 (SMR (1989) file). (Fredengren 2002, KILC 027).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the water, but merging with the W shore of Lough Gara. A low-cairn crannog (12m N-S; 12m E-W; H 0.81m above the lake-bed), the surface of which consists of firmly set stones. The edges of the crannog slope down distinctly to the S, but more gradually to the N. Two stone-built jetties lead from the NE corner out into the water. The northern jetty (L 7.7m; Wth 1.4m) consists of large stones (diam. c. 0.7m) on top of smaller ones. The other jetty (L 5m; Wth 1.2m) consists of small stones. Another crannog (SL044-092----) lies c. 20m to S. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILC 025).

source_data.original_text:
In wet stony pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A roughly circular area (int. diam. 33m x 35m) enclosed by a drystone wall (T 1.5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.6m). The wall has a rubble core with internal and external stone facing and a basal course of large boulders. Except for the N arc, the wall is ruinous and covered with overgrowth. The interior is very overgrown with trees and bushes. Recorded in 1836 as 'Caisiol, a stone fort. There was formerly an old building in the townland called Caisiol in Irish' (OSNB vol. 1, 479). Several stone field boundaries adjoin the cashel.

source_data.original_text:
In a clearing in a hazel wood on the N shore of Lough Gara and c. 15m E of a road. A roughly rectangular flat-topped sandstone boulder (0.95m NW-SE; 0.75m NE-SW; H 0.35m) embedded in the ground. There are two depressions on its upper surface, to NW and SE of the centre respectively. The NW depression is circular (diam. c. 0.35m) and very shallow and contains a pile of small coins. The U-shaped SE depression (L 0.5m; Wth 0.28m; D 0.21m) is natural and extends to the edge of the stone. Several faint linear striations, including a small cross, occur to the E of the U-shaped depression though some of these may be natural. Local tradition associates the stone with St Patrick and it is said that the depressions were formed when the saint rested on the stone. An ecclesiastical enclosure (SL045-011003-), within which are a church (SL045-011001-) and graveyard (SL045-011002-) and the site of a leacht cuimhne (SL045-011004-), lies c. 600m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On the top of a hill. Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and as 'Rock scribing\art possible'. The rock is known locally as the 'Danes Rock' and marks on it are thought to have been made by the Danes while sharpening their swords (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). However, no rock art is visible on the exposed surfaces of the rock; striations, aligned NE-SW, are likely to be of glacial origin.

In rough pasture, on a level terrace close to break of slope, on the NE side of a stream valley. A dense hazel and holly wood borders the cashel to S and SW and an impenetrable band of blackthorn bushes conceals the enclosing wall N-SE. A roughly circular area (c. 21m N-S; c. 22m ENE-WSW) enclosed by a drystone wall (Wth 1.4m; int. H 1.3m; ext. H 1.3m). The wall is most substantial NW-SE where it serves as a property boundary. There is a break (Wth 0.6m) in the bank at NW and several low areas in the tumbled wall SE-S. The interior is densely overgrown with hazel and blackthorn though a scattering of loose stones covering the surface is evident. Field boundaries radiate out from the cashel wall at N, SE, S, W and NW. A small rectangular hut site (SL046-021001-) lies c. 3m to SE and another cashel (SL046-020----) lies c. 80m to W.

source_data.original_text:
In the water, just outside the S shore of Sroove townland in the W side of Lough Gara. A low-cairn crannog (12m N-S; 10m E-W; H 0.9-1.1m above the lake-bed), surrounded by rushes, consisting mainly of large angular flagstones (diam. c. 0.5m) with some medium-sized boulders on the surface. These stones are loosely set into the white marl of the crannog body and the surface is quite uneven. The edge is clearly defined in material. At least 12 eroded vertical posts surround the crannog. There is an intermittent causeway of flagstones resting on lake-marl leading in towards the shoreline. The water depth around the crannog is 0.7m and only 0.4m of the crannog is above water. The crannog has been radiocarbon-dated to the early medieval period (Fredengren 2002, KILC 020). (Cross 1953, fig. 1).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a meadow in the W side of Lough Gara between the former shoreline and the present summer waterline. This crannog was excavated in 1997-2000 by the Crannog Research Programme and is now reconstructed (Fredengren 1998b, 156; 2000a, 185; 2000b, 282-3). Prior to excavation the crannog was very overgrown and consisted of a low cairn (17m N-S; 14m E-W; H 1.05m above the meadow). The top layer consisted of poorly sorted angular boulders and flagstones forming an unstable surface. A causeway (L 16m; Wth 1m) of boulders stretches W from the crannog to the former shoreline and from the E edge out into the water for 68m. This part of the causeway consists mainly of small shattered stones (diam. c. 0.05-0.1m). Excavation revealed an early medieval multiphase construction which showed evidence for house structures, a lower-status artefact assemblage and some evidence for metal production (Fredengren 1998a, 31-3; 2002, 220-46). It has been radiocarbon-dated to the early medieval period (Fredengren 2002, KILC 022). It is one of a group of three crannogs (SL046-027----; SL046-028----). (Cross 1953, fig. 1).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On rolling pasture about 600m W of Lough Gara. A W-facing gallery (min. L 6.7m) is divided by a septal-stone into a portico and main chamber and is surrounded by the remains of an outer-wall. The structure, which is built with quite small orthostats, stands in a low mound (10m E-W; max. 8m N-S; H 0.5m). The portico (L 1.5m) is formed by two stones at the S and another, now fallen, at the N side. The septal-stone is broken in two pieces. Between the N end of the septal-stone and the N side of the main chamber there is a small stone. The main chamber (min. L 5m; Wth 1.2m at septal-stone, 0.9m towards opposite end) is represented by six stones to the N and five to the S. At the inner end of the S side there is a partly buried stone of uncertain function. There is a displaced stone about mid-way along the main chamber. The outer-wall at the N is represented by seven stones and that at the S also by seven stones. A partly buried stone immediately outside the easternmost outer-wall stone at the S seems to be prostrate. The back of the outer-walling is represented by a single orthostat. Two facade-stones, both fallen to W, linked the southern outer-wall to the front of the portico. A single facade-stone, a thin slab, stands just forward of the northern outer-wall. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 80-81, no. 127)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In a wet meadow, below the former shoreline, in a shallow bay on the W shore of Lough Gara. The crannog is surrounded by flat ground with views of the Curlew Mountains. In pasture, at the E end of a low elevation on the shores of Lough Gara. A roughly D-shaped area (dims. 43.5m N-S) with a straight SSE side (L c. 55m ENE-WSW) is defined SSW-NW by a broad low rise of earth and stone (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.65m) topped by hazel and blackthorn bushes, by a slight grassy rise NNW-NE and by a low stony scarp (H 0.55m) obscured by overgrowth NE-ESE. The straight SSE side is defined by a broadly sloping scarp (H 0.7m) covered with a tumble of stones, probably the remains of stone facing. Sections of a stone-faced scarp can be seen elsewhere along the immediate shoreline. The interior slopes slightly down to SSE; a slight linear depression (Wth c. 1.5m) which extends E-W across the N half may be the remains of a drain. The perimeter of the enclosure is engulfed in hazel, blackthorn and bramble scrub, almost impenetrable in places.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle N-facing slope c. 100m NW of a graveyard (SL046-026001-). This well is named ‘St. Patrick’s Well’ on the 1838 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. Inspection was difficult due to dense overgrowth of hawthorn bushes and brambles, and it is now enclosed by a timber fence. It consists of a roughly circular straight-sided pit (diam. c. 2m; D c. 0.5m) with some stones protruding from the sides. The base of the pit holds a little water. According to local information, it was accessed on the SE side where the slope is gentle. There is a tradition that St Brigid knelt to pray here and her knee prints can still be seen on a stone at the well.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Lough Gara, at the edge of the reeds and surrounded by flat land. This site consists of a number of features connected together by spreads of stone and boulders varying in size. The main feature is a possible crannog (13.4m N-S; 7.2m E-W; H 0.9m above the lake-bed; H 0.3m above the water) and it is furthermost into the water. To its W there are small angular stones (diam. c. 0.05m), well-set into the ground while to E there is a substantial amount of large angular boulders (diam. 0.5-1m) and also smaller stones and gravel. The edges are clear against the lake-bed sediments. It is connected to the shoreline by a causeway of intermittent boulders. Adjacent to the crannog is an elongated feature, possibly a causeway harbour arm. The vegetation consists of one tree, two shrubs and patches of grass. (Fredengren 2002, KILC 016-18)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In Lough Gara, on the S shore of Inch Island, with views of Mullaghtee and another crannog (SL047-021----) c. 1.3km to E, between Inch Island and Derrymore Island. In the water outside the present and an earlier shoreline on a lake-bed of marl and connected to the shore by a causeway of soil. A low-cairn crannog (22.9m N-S; 20.8m E-W; H 1.94m) with a thin grass cover and a few nettles growing on it. There is a mid-cairn (8.1m N-S; 7.2m E-W) in the N half consisting of well-set angular and subangular stones, mainly sandstone with occasional limestone. A plateau (Wth 2.6-6.2m), consisting of densely packed stones, surrounds the mid-cairn. The edge of the crannog is distinct in material and drops quite sharply into the lake where the stones seem to be capping the marl. Vertical wooden posts surround the crannog. An additional area (6m N-S, 2m E-W) of packed stones is evident on the NW corner, where the crannog joins the low causeway. This crannog has been radiocarbon-dated to the Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age (Fredengren 2002, KILA 016). Another crannog (SL047-004001-) lies c. 100m to E. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2000c, 26; 2002, KILA 016)


The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In Lough Gara, on the NE shore of Inch Island with views over the mouth of the Boyle River and to the Ox Mountains. The two possible crannogs (SL047-006----; SL047-007----) (Cross 1953, fig. 1) have become indistinct with no definite edges. They consist mainly of wooden posts in an area where water has eroded out sediments and exposed the white lake marl. Overlying the marl is a number of small angular stones. The older shoreline is visible further up on the shore. During the site inspection twenty-six pieces of wood were found in the shallow water and also wooden posts, horizontal timbers and pieces of brushwood, directly on top of or in the marl. Further up towards the older shoreline there are rows of stones, firmly set into the ground. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 014, 015)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a S-facing slope on Derrymore Island in Lough Gara. A raised circular area (int. diam. 20m) enclosed by two banks and an intervening waterlogged fosse (Wth 6m) which is best evident along the W arc. The inner bank is earthen but degraded (Wth 2m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1m) while the outer bank is of earth and stone (Wth 2.5m; int. H 1.55m; ext. H 1.3m). This rath overlooks a complex of eight possible crannogs (SL047-012002-; SL047-012003; SL047-012004-; SL047-012005-; SL047-012006-; SL047-012007-; SL047-012008-; SL047-012009) and one crannog (SL047-012001-), all to SE.

source_data.original_text:
Off the point of Rathtinaun drumlin on the E side of Lough Gara and almost submerged. This crannog has an unusual exposed mid-lake position, has good views and is intervisible with another crannog (SL047-021----) and a possible crannog (SL047-016----) to SE and NE respectively. The surface of the crannog (10.3m N-S; 11.3m E-W; H 1.3m above the lake mud) consists of a number of flagstones (max. dim. 0.8m) placed on smaller angular and subangular stones, mainly sandstone. The body of the crannog consists of a dense concentration of loosely packed stones. The surface is uneven with no soil visible. To E of the centre, the flagstones form an almost stepped surface. Three submerged wooden posts were observed, protruding up through the stone packing. The site appears to have definite edges, possibly less distinct to the W, sloping sharply to W and E. The stones seem to be resting on white lake marl in which fragments of wood were noted. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 020)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
