source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow, below the former shoreline of Lough Gara. It is surrounded by drumlins and therefore views are restricted. This high-cairn crannog, was excavated by Joseph Raftery between 1953 and 1955 (Raftery 1957, 10-15; Raftery 1994, 32-5) and prior to excavation was described as a large cairn or mound (36m x 29m; H 2.5m). The excavation showed that the crannog contained layers from the Late Bronze Age through to the medieval period. The base seemed to have been constructed by the piling of timbers and brushwood on a slight rise in the lake-bed. The Bronze Age levels contained a number of fireplaces. A hoard was found outside the crannog consisting of a wooden box in which were a necklace of amber beads, rings of bronze, tin and lead, tweezers, a bronze pin and six boar tusks. A dugout boat was found lying on the lake-bed beside the crannog (O'Sullivan 1998, 118). The crannog is now evident as a horseshoe-shaped cairn (25m N-S; 22.8m E-W; H c. 2.5m) with a scooped-out interior (10m N-S; 17.3m E-W), in the centre of which is a water-filled hollow (5.9m N-S; 11.7m E-W), probably resulting from the excavation. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; O'Sullivan 1998, 118-21; Fredengren 2002, KILA 018)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 213/1955).

source_data.original_text:
In an inlet of Lough Gara, on marshy ground; views of the open lake are restricted due to the surrounding drumlins. In summer the surrounding area consists of a grassy water meadow. This crannog is covered with undergrowth and a number of mature trees, making inspection difficult. It is a high-cairn crannog (52m N-S; 44m E-W; max. H 2.8m above the meadow) with a central mid-cairn (12m N-S, 10m E-W; H 0.7m) consisting of grass-covered stones. The edge of this mid-cairn is most distinct along the S arc. It is surrounded by a plateau (Wth c. 8m), consisting of small subangular stones. The plateau is distinct to N, W and S but barely discernible to E. A wide berm (Wth 10-12m) surrounds the plateau. In the E portion of the berm is a hollow (5.2m N-S; 6m E-W; D 0.6m) with gently sloping sides. On the S edge of the berm is a low flat bank or wall (Wth 4m; int. H 0.3m). At NE is a ridge which though very overgrown shows a high sand content. It projects to NE as a point. The stone-packing on this site is at all levels compact and grass-covered with the stones being firmly set. There is less vegetation cover on the berm. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 034)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a water-meadow, below the earlier shoreline of Lough Gara, on the S side of the Ross peninsula. Views to the N, E and S are blocked by drumlins; Mullaghtee and Monasteraden are visible across the lake to the W. A drain to the SW shows the surrounding meadow to consist of peat on sand and marl. A low-cairn crannog (14.8m N-S; 14.8m E-W; H 1m above water meadow) sparsely covered with low grass and nettles and with two hawthorn trees on its N side. It consists mainly of firmly set stones. In the NE quadrant is an area (4m x 4m) containing a dense concentration of stones. The W side of this concentration contains somewhat larger limestone and sandstone stones (diam. c. 0.3m) while the E side contains a slightly higher concentration of shattered sandstone (diam. 0.05-0.1m). The crannog slopes down towards the lake. In the NW quadrant is a loosely packed dense concentration (2m x 3m) of moss-covered sandstone stones (diam. 0.3-0.4m). The edge is distinct in material and has a sharp angle down to the meadow. There is very limited overspill of stones from the cairn. The even surface slopes gently down towards the lake and consists of well sorted, firmly set small stones (diam. c. 0.2m). The crannog is surrounded by water in winter. One of a group of four crannogs (SL047-055----; SL047-056001-; SL047-057----) in the same bay. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 048)


The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on top of and occupying almost the entire width of a narrow ridge with panoramic views and overlooking another rath (SL047-060----), c. 200m to NE. The rath is indicated as an oval enclosure on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. It is now evident as a slightly raised, roughly D-shaped area (25.5m N-S; 23m E-W) defined at W by a linear NNE-SSW field boundary which truncates the W arc. The interior is defined NNW-SSW by a scarp (H 1.05m) with a slight internal lip (H 0.3m). The scarp (H 1.4m) NNW-NE is incorporated into a second field boundary. There is an eroded gap (Wth 2m) in the scarp at SE. The interior is level and grass-covered and the perimeter is ringed with hawthorn and brambles. A slight hollow around the base of the scarp, noted during a previous inspection in 1993 (SMR (1989) file), is no longer evident.

In pasture, in a flat valley, overlooked to SSW by a ridge. A roughly circular area (49.8m ESE-WNW; c. 47.5m NNE-SSW) enclosed by the remains of two earthen banks with an intervening and external fosse. The inner bank (Wth 5.4m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1.8m) is evident SSE-NNW, with remnants E-ESE, is levelled NNW-NE and is truncated by a N-S field boundary ENE-E. The intervening fosse (Wth 3.5m) and substantial outer bank (Wth 4.4m; int. H 1.7m; ext. H 1.2m) are evident SSE-SW. The intervening fosse is flat-bottomed, waterlogged and marked by rushes. The external fosse (Wth 3m; D 0.4m) is evident SSE-SW as a broad shallow depression marked by rushes. A slight rise (Wth c. 1.5m), highlighted by a differential growth pattern, on the outer edge of the external fosse at SSE may be remnants of a counterscarp bank. The interior slopes gently down to NNE. At SSE there is a poorly defined gap (Wth 2.4m) in the inner bank, a causeway (Wth 4m) across the intervening fosse and a corresponding gap in the outer bank, though the latter is now marked only by the E terminal of the outer bank. There is a stream/drain immediately to N of the rath. Another rath (SL047-059----) is c. 200m to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the S side of Derrymore Island in Lough Gara. In pasture, at the break of slope of a wooded scarp bordering the lakeshore. A rectangular area (27m N-S; 43.5m E-W), with rounded NE and NW corners, defined on the W, N and E sides by an earthen bank (Wth 2.4m; int. H 0.35m; ext. H 0.4m). The S side is defined by a scarp (H c. 1.3m) which merges with the steep natural slope (H c. 3.5m) down to the lakeshore. Midway along the bank on the N side is a small rectangular outward projection (c. 2m N-S; 7.5m E-W). There are breaks in the bank at W (Wth 5.7m), N (Wth 3.7m) and NE (Wth 3m). Outside the bank at the N end of the E side is a shallow wet depression (Wth c. 2m) marked by a growth of rushes. The interior slopes down gently from the centre to S and is crossed, off-centre to E, by a N-S field boundary. Hawthorn, blackthorn and hazel bushes cover the perimeter, much of the E third of the interior and the slope to S. A circular enclosure (SL047-010001-) is c. 50m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a small marshy inlet, on the E shores of Lough Gara. Discovered in 1991 during monitoring of drainage works at the foreshore (Wren 1991) when a small section (2.7m N-S; 8.7m E-W) was exposed. Described as a tightly packed spread of undressed limestone and red sandstone blocks (dims. 0.1-0.4m) surrounded by a 1.3m wide band of post-holes (diam. 0.1-0.2m) (ibid.). The blocks were set in a rough concentration with a definite edge evident at NW and small strips of wood (some burnt) and hazelnuts were found in the sand and marl around the stones (Wren 1991). There are now no visible remains of this crannog.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In damp, rush-grown pasture, located on the S bank of a stream/field drain that flows E through a small valley. A field bank borders the N edge of the stream/field drain. 
Low, roughly D-shaped mound (8.5m N−S; c. 13m E−W), visible as a green, grassy rise in a dense sea of rushes. It is cut on its straight side at N by the roughly E-W field drain (Wth 1.2m at top, 0.6m at base; D 1.3m below top of mound). The mound is low profile; it is highest along its N edge where it borders the stream/drain, grading down gently from there to S where it barely rises above surrounding ground level.  
Another field ditch (Wth c. 1m), on a NE−SW axis, cuts through the E half of the mound, expanding to c. 2m in width at NE, close to the point at which it intersects with the E−W stream/drain. It is possible that this expanded area incorporates part of an original trough hollow. This portion of the burnt mound is denuded of sod and eroded, revealing a concentration of angular stone fragments in black, charcoal-rich soil.

source_data.original_text:
In Moygara Castle (SL044-052001-). Listed in the SMR (1989) and in the RMP (1995) where it is classified as 'Sheela-na-gig' and 'Stone sculpture' respectively. According to Wakeman this carving was that of sheela-na-gig which was located on the barbican of Moygara Castle (SL044-052001-) (Wakeman 1880, 282; Guest 1936, 111).  Described by Guest as a ‘limestone block, on the corbelled end of which the figure is rudely carved, now lies on the ground near the castle entrance’ (Guest 1936, 111).  The carving displays certain affinities with exhibitionist figures though the nature of the remains hardly permits classification as such with any degree of certainty and some caution is necessary in proposing this interpretation (Cherry 1992, 9).  Another keystone (SL044-052003-) lies nearby and it has an equally worn carving, possibly of two figures facing each other (SMR (1989) file). 

Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien and Paul Walsh
Date of upload/revision: 23 May 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, immediately to SW of the village of Monasteraden, located on a gentle SE-facing slope, overlooking Lough Gara to the S.
The remains of 'Cashelnamonastragh', consist of a roughly circular enclosure (77m E-W; c. 71m N-S) defined by a low flat-topped sod-covered rise (Wth c. 2m; H c. 0.5m) on top of which the enclosing wall of Monasterredan graveyard (SL046-014002-) is built. The sod-covered rise projects from under the internal wall-face of the graveyard NW-NE and from under its external face NE-ESE. It is truncated at SE by a cottage garden and by an access road. The graveyard wall respects the outer edge of the rise S-W. There is a souterrain (SL046-014004-) in the NW quadrant of the interior, a corn-drying kiln (SL046-014008-) in the interior at WSW and a bullaun stone (SL046-014005-) immediately outside the enclosure at NNE. The precise location of a cross-slab (SL046-014007-), which was found in the interior, is not known. In 1836 the enclosure was recorded as a 'cashel' though 'very little of it remains' (OSL, 419).
Little is known about this early ecclesiastical foundation. Based on the placename ‘Monasteredan’, O’Rorke (1889, vol. 2, 380-1) speculated that this is the site of a monastery founded by St Aidan, possibly Aedhán Ó Fiachrach who died in AD 570, a theory repeated by Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 398). However, recent research has refuted this interpretation of the placename: The historical evidence suggests that the name derives from either ‘Mainistir Raodáin’ or the local version recorded in 1836 ‘Mainistir Réudáin’, standardised to Mainistir Réadáin by the first placenames order in 1975. O’Rorke’s theory, therefore, is not supported by the placename evidence, and, in this regard, it is notable that a connection with Saint Aodhán was not recorded locally during the course of the 1836 Ordnance Survey (Pers. Comm. 2020: Dr. Conchubhar Ó Crualaoich, The Placenames Branch, DCHG).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of revised upload: 17 February 2020

A roughly circular area (c. 7m NE-SW; c. 7m NW-SE) defined NNW-NE by an arc of an earth and stone bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.85m; ext. H 0.35m) with a broad internal slump, ESE-S by remnants of a linear scarp that follows the break of slope and S-W by a low stony rise. The NNW terminal is broader and higher than the remainder and incorporates some large stones, possibly from field clearance. There are breaks in the bank at NW (Wth 2m) and E (Wth 2.7m). There is a field boundary wall immediately to E. A standing stone (SL046-051002-) lies c. 30m to W.

source_data.original_text:
On a slight prominence in undulating pasture, overlooked by higher ground to S but with extensive views N-SE and overlooking Lough Gara to SE. Moygara Castle consists of a square bawn (L 51m) enclosed by a curtain wall with a tower at each corner, a gate-tower in the centre of the W side, and the lower courses of a rectangular structure along the inside of the N wall (see plan in Casey 1992). The entire complex is built of uncoursed rubble stone in a lime mortar. 
The earliest part of the complex would appear to be the rectangular structure (17m E-W; 12.5m N-S) which stands on the N side of the bawn, its N wall roughly on the same line as the curtain wall. This structure appears to pre-date the curtain wall as the curtain is butted up against its NW corner; the junction with the curtain wall at the NE corner is obscured by collapsed rubble. The only evident intact feature of the rectangular structure is a vertical shaft (1.4m x 0.65m) just inside its NW corner, which is probably the shaft for a garderobe. Otherwise the structure is largely reduced to an uneven mound of rubble covered by sod. 
The curtain wall stands close to full height (average H 3.3m; T 1.24m) but is now topped by a sod layer with no indication of the original finish. Along all four walls, just above present ground level, are roughly evenly spaced gun loops: five in the N wall; ten in the E wall; thirteen in the S wall; and ten in the W wall. These loops are plain lintelled embrasures splayed from a small rectangular opening in the exterior wall-face (int. Wth c. 0.55m; int. H c. 0.7m; H of opening c. 0.2m; Wth of opening c. 0.15m). Some loops look straight through the wall whilst others are angled. Along certain sections of the curtain, the top of the inner face is brought forward by two oversailing courses; this widening of the wall top accommodated a wall walk. 
The wall is interrupted in three places: a gate-tower in the centre of the W wall; a breach in the centre of the E wall; and along the rectangular structure in the N wall. The gate-tower stood to at least two storeys but is now very ruinous; the structure is butt-built against the inside face of the curtain wall and is therefore later in date than the curtain. However, the front doorway (Wth 2.2m) is in the thickness of the curtain wall and is probably contemporary with it. Only the basal jambs of the outer door surround survive; these have a chamfered edge and a plain stop-chamfer. The door was secured by two drawbars, the sockets of which survive. Lying on the ground here are two limestone keystones (SL044-052002-, SL044-052003-); each has a carving on its outside face but these are now almost worn beyond recognition. One appears to be two figures facing each other whilst the other is a single figure holding something in its arms (SMR (1989) file). Neither of these appears to be the figure of a sheela-na-gig though Guest (1936, 111 and fig. 7) implies that one might be. Inside the doorway is rectangular lobby (3.2m x 2.5m) on the N side of which was a smaller subsidiary chamber that is now almost entirely ruined. The plain round rear archway (Wth 2.15m), which gave access into the bawn, is partially fallen. Roughly in the centre of the E curtain wall is a featureless breach (Wth c. 3m) which is probably recent.
The four corner towers are similar in plan and layout but the SW tower stands to three storeys whereas the other three stand only to two. In plan all are slightly angled towards the outside corner in bastion fashion but this angle is very slight and none of the gun loops are positioned to cover the angle with flanking fire. All the door and window frames and the embrasure lintels were made of wood, none of these survive and their absence now greatly weakens the structures. The SW tower's roughly square ground-floor chamber (int. L 5.1m) is entered directly through a doorway from the SW corner of the bawn. The room has no windows but contains seven gun loops, one looking along the outside face of the S curtain wall, and another pair looking along the inside and outside face of the W curtain. The first-floor room is also entered directly through a doorway from the SW corner of the bawn. This room is lit by a window in each wall and was heated by a fireplace in the centre of its W wall. It also contains an array of gun loops, three of which are placed in a central projection in the E wall, overlooking the S curtain wall. The second floor is arranged in a similar fashion but there is no doorway so that entry must have been via an internal wooden staircase. The parapet is embattled with low plain rectangular merlons pierced by very small gun loops. There is a narrow wall walk-along the inside edge. The other three towers are all similarly laid out but with variation in the position of windows, fireplaces and loops. None of these towers now stand higher than two storeys but as none preserve any wall-top features it is unclear if any of them ever stood higher. 
An additional rectangular structure stood inside the bawn at its SW corner (c. 15m N-S; c. 8m E-W). This is now almost entirely reduced to rubble but is a late addition as its walls butt against the inside face of the curtain and one end partially blocked a gun loop. 
Moygara Castle was one of the chief residences of the O'Garas (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 364-6; Wood-Martin 1882, 99-100). It was attacked by the O'Donnells in 1538, and again in 1581 by 'a body of mercenary Scots' who burned the buildings (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 364-6). The present complex, excluding the rectangular structure on the N side which is probably the stump of a late medieval tower-house, is probably late 16th/early 17th-century in date judging by the window forms, the proliferation of gun loops and the bastion-like angle of the corner towers. It may be the result of a rebuilding after the attack of 1581.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low terrace from which the ground slopes down gently for c. 50m to the shores of Lough Gara; just S of the centre of Temple-Ronaun graveyard (SL045-011002-), within the SE quadrant of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL045-011003-). A ruined rectangular church (ext. dims. 10.35m ESE-WNW; 6.3m NNE-SSW) with walls (T 0.75m) of large coursed sandstone blocks, that are in poor structural condition and partially overgrown with ivy. The S wall is the highest (max. H 2.4m) but it has a large bulge in the centre of its external face. The N and E walls (max. H 1.3m) show evidence of rough rebuilding in places. Only the basal courses of the W wall remain, on top of which are roughly piled displaced stones. A gap at the N end of this wall may indicate the position of the doorway. The proportions and construction suggest an early medieval date for the church. Modern graves occupy about half of the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Within the SE quadrant of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL045-011003-). A rectangular area (48.6m WNW-ESE; 38.2m NNE-SSW) enclosed by a modern stone wall with a recent extension to the E (18m WNW-ESE) enclosed by a concrete wall. The church (SL045-011001-) is just S of the centre of the interior. A drop in ground level in the S third of the graveyard, c. 4m S of the church, is marked by a scarp (H 0.5m) which extends E-W across the full length of the graveyard. The majority of headstones date to the late 19th and 20th centuries but interspersed amongst them are several uninscribed grave-markers, some in N-S rows. In the W half are five small rectangular grave-plots (the largest measuring 8.4m x 5.65m) defined by roughly built drystone walls (H c. 0.8m) incorporating some stones possibly robbed from the church and, according to local information, some stone from a leacht cuimhne (SL045-011004-). Attached to the wall of one of these grave-plots is a late 18th/ early 19th-century plaque (Wth 0.45m; H 0.87m), with the dates of 1732 and 1733 (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney), depicting the crucifixion above a coat of arms. In 1836 it was recorded that the graveyard was known as 'Temple-Ronaun' (OSNB vol. 1, 490) which is pronounced 'Teampul Ronan' (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a gentle slope, with a view of the Curlew Mountains to N. Excavated in 1973 by Wallace (1974, 23-4) who described 'two roughly concentric rings of orthostats, the diameters of which were 14.5m and 8m', the inner and outer retaining walls for a 'ring-cairn of loosely placed stones' the height of which would have been at least 1.7m. The inner circular area was empty except for a segment in the SE quadrant which contained two short cists (SL046-003002-; SL046-003003-) covered by a thin layer of cairn stones and revetted by a low crescent-shaped setting of small orthostats. The soil under the cairn stones was flecked with charcoal. The site is now evident as a kidney-shaped sod-covered cairn (4.3m x 3m). (Waddell 1990, 133)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

One of two short cists (see SL046-003003-) found in the SE quadrant of a ring-cairn (SL046-003001-) (Wallace 1974, 23-4), both of which were covered by a thin layer of cairn stones and revetted by a low crescent-shaped setting of small orthostats. Excavation revealed a rectangular cist, built of sandstone slabs with other slabs flanking N and E sides, and capped by a simple capstone. This cist had three floors, each consisting of a horizontal layer of large flat sandstone paving stones. The lowermost floor covered a deposit of hazelnuts arranged in a pit, on top of and partly surrounded by cremated human bone. The main burial was that of a child and was found on the topmost floor accompanied by two sherds of food-vessel pottery. The second cist was found a short distance to the SW. (Waddell 1990, 133; Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 131)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a SE-facing slope. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a circular enclosure with two deciduous trees in the interior. Described in 1994 as a circular area (int. diam. 20m N-S; 21.1m E-W) defined by remnants of a sod-covered stone wall (Wth 3.9m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.2m) (SMR (1989) file). Subsequently further damage to the cashel has occurred. A field boundary wall now crosses the interior on a ENE-WSW axis, slightly S of centre and there are now no visible remains of the cashel at ground level on the S side of this wall, apart from an area of rough ground which extends 6m to S. On the N side of the wall a semicircular area (c. 15m N-S; c. 24m E-W) is defined by a low sod-covered rise (Wth c. 3m; ext. H 0.35m) WSW-NW and NE-ENE. Mature beech trees grow along both of these rises and stones are evident in places under the roots of the trees. A depression (Wth 1.5-2m; D 0.2m) on the internal side of the enclosing rise WSW-NW, terminating at its NW end in a large heap of stones, was possibly used to facilitate the recent removal of stones. The N two-thirds of the interior are level while the S third sloped down to SE. There is a souterrain (SL046-012002-) in the NW quadrant.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the E side of a road, and on a S-facing slope, at the point where a stream emerges from underground. The well is partially enclosed by a stone wall, part of which is of recent construction. A crucifixion plaque (SL046-013002-) dated to the 1660s is set into the wall at the N side of the well and several rounded 'cursing stones' (SL046-013004-) are cemented on top of the wall above the plaque. The well, which is approached from the road by roughly made stone steps at S, is roughly circular (2.1m N-S; 2.3m E-W; D c. 1m) and mostly lined with drystone walling, though incorporating bedrock in places. A bullaun stone (SL046-013003-) projects from the enclosing wall at NNE into the well space, just above the water level. The drystone wall is topped with a mortared stone wall. The stream exits from the well through a low lintelled opening at W and is channelled out into an adjoining subsidiary well. The subsidiary well which is open to S, is roughly square (0.8m N-S; 0.9m E-W) with stone walls and a single roofing lintel. Upon exiting the subsidiary well the stream flows SE for 3m in an open stone-lined drain and then into the adjoining field to E. The well is traditionally associated with St Attracta and the pattern day is held on 11th August. According to Wood-Martin (1892, 368) 'the altar and walls were some years ago restored by the nuns of Ballaghadereen'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the N side of a holy well (SL046-013001-), set into a stone wall on top of which is a set of cursing stones (SL046-013004-). The plaque consists of a limestone slab (H 0.51m; Wth 0.31m) on which is carved a crucifixion scene in relief. The arms of the cross extend the full width of the slab while the base of the shaft terminates on a low plinth. The head of the Christ figure is disproportionately large with simplified facial features while the hair and beard have been depicted with considerable attention to detail. Several symbols of the crucifixion are also depicted including a ladder and a bird as well as instruments of the passion, some of which are partially eroded. The plaque is centrally placed in the wall facade and is flanked on each side by two large vertically set limestone slabs. The slab immediately to the right bears a now worn inscription which was read by Wood-Martin (1892, 368) as 'IHS 1662 11. 1: G'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
The graveyard is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as polygonal in plan while on the 1914 OS 6-inch map it is indicated as oval in plan. The remains consist of an oval area (76.4m E-W; 68.7m N-S) enclosed by a mortared stone wall (Wth 0.45m; H 1m). There is an arched gateway at SE, above which is a date plaque inscribed '1883'. The headstones are mostly 20th century in date and are accessed by concrete paths. Scattered amongst them are several small uninscribed grave-markers, mostly rectangular though a few are roughly cross-shaped. A graveslab (SL046-014007-) with a simple incised cross on it, which was within the interior, cannot be located. A low stone-built seat (1.5m N-S; 1.26m E-W; H 0.45m), in an area of rough uneven ground close to the enclosing wall at WSW, marks the location of a corn-drying kiln (SL046-014008-), which was found here during a graveyard clean-up in 1985-6. The N half of the interior is level with the external ground level while the S half is raised c. 0.6m above it. The exact location of the site of the church (SL046-014001-) is unknown though the most likely location is the central area, surrounded by a path, where few graves occur (pers. comm. J. Enright). There is a souterrain (SL046-014004-) in the NW quadrant and a bullaun stone (SL046-014005-) outside the enclosing wall at NNE. A quernstone (SL046-014006-) was also found in the graveyard. In 1836 this graveyard was recorded as 'a burial ground for children, strangers and poor people' (OSL, 235) and was then only in occasional use (OSNB vol. 1, 414).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a S-facing slope overlooking Lough Gara. A roughly circular area (35m N-S; 33.5m E-W) enclosed by an inner sod-covered drystone wall, an intervening fosse and an outer earth and stone bank. The inner wall (max. Wth 2m; H 1.6m) is evident all round though not of uniform width suggesting some rebuilding especially NE-ESE (Wth 1.4m). In places, most noticeably N-NE, the external face of the wall has collapsed outwards. There are narrow gaps in the wall at W (Wth 0.4m) and NE (Wth 0.6m). The outer enclosing element consists of a stony scarp (H 0.4m) N-NE, a bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.4m) NE-S and a slight rise (Wth c. 2m) marked by bushes and ferns S-W. There are no visible remains of the outer bank or fosse W-N. The intervening fosse, which is evident N-W, is not noticeably sunken anywhere and from N-NE is a stony terrace (Wth c. 1.4m) covered by a surface spread of stone tumble and E-ESE is a level grassy strip (Wth 4m) marginally higher than the external ground level. The interior is mostly level and dotted with clumps of ferns, brambles and bushes and a moderate scattering of loose stones. The NW quadrant is slightly raised and defined by a slight scarp (H 0.3m) on NNE-SSW axis. In the NE quadrant, two roughly linear heaps of loose stones, at right angles to each other, generally define an area (c. 9m N-S; 9m E-W) of slightly sunken ground. Immediately to S, and just E of the centre of the cashel, is a roughly oval cairn (3m N-S; 4.6m E-W; max. source_data.original_text:
On a gentle S-facing slope, on a narrow peninsula in Lough Gara. A subrectangular area (c. 100m E-W; c. 60m N-S) defined on the E and W sides by field boundaries, on the S side by a scarp (H c. 1m) and on the N side by a low relict field boundary. The interior is grass-covered. In the NW quadrant is the outline of a rectangular enclosure (c. 35-40m N-S; 30m E-W), which was indicated by a broken line on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. It is defined on the E and W sides by a low sod-covered rise (Wth 1.4m; H 0.3m), on the S side by a low scarp obscured by overgrowth while its N side is open. In the S half of this enclosure is another smaller rectangular area (13m N-S; 11.8m E-W) which is enclosed by a collapsed stone wall. There is a penitential station (SL046-026002-) with a collection of praying stones (SL046-026004-) on its upper surface, in the SW quadrant of this latter area. In general, the interior of the smaller rectangular area has an uneven stony surface but there are a few small upright slabs, probably grave-markers. A shallow oblong sunken area (9m N-S; 6m E-W) with a shallow linear depression (Wth 1m) extending from its S end, lies in the NE quadrant. The remains of a corn-drying kiln (SL046-026003-) are on the S side. St Patrick's well (SL046-044----) lies c. 100m to the NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the W half of Annagh graveyard (SL046-026001-) and within the SW quadrant of a small subrectangular enclosure (11.8m E-W; 13m N-S). Named 'Altar' on the 1838 and 1914 OS 6-inch maps. It consists of a drystone-built rectangular platform (1.25m N-S; 1.4m E-W; H 0.4m at N side; 0.68m at S side) composed of roughly coursed horizontally laid limestone and sandstone slabs. It is built up on the S side to compensate for the sloping ground. Its upper surface is covered with a loose jumble of stones, mostly irregular but including several water-rolled cobbles which are known locally as 'praying stones' (SL046-026004-). A possible bullaun stone (SL046-026005-) was traditionally kept here. There is also a wedge-shaped sandstone slab (L 0.85m; Wth 0.28-0.47m; T 0.09m) incorporated into the upper surface of the platform at the SE corner and a sandstone slab (L 1m; Wth 0.3m; T 0.13m) lies prostrate on the ground 1m to N. The 'altar' is similar to that known as 'The Big Station' on Inishmurray island, county Sligo (see Harbison 1991, fig. 37). It is now surrounded by a post and barbed wire fence.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, just below the summit of a ridge, on a S-facing slope. A roughly oval area (30.7m N-S; 26.4m E-W) enclosed by a roughly coursed drystone wall. From NE-S the wall (T 2.5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.4m) is least modified. Elsewhere sections of it have been breached, modified or rebuilt or obscured by accumulations of field-clearance stones. At NW stones have been piled on top of the wall and a slump of loose stones has spilled into the interior, possibly a mixture of wall collapse and field-clearance stones. A section of wall (L c. 5m) at N has been breached and partially rebuilt. A field boundary extends N from the cashel wall immediately E of this breach while immediately E of the field boundary another section of the wall (L 11m) has been rebuilt and expanded into the interior to form a D-shaped structure. Immediately E of this structure is a narrow break (Wth 1.05m) in the cashel wall. A further blocked-up gap (Wth 1.8m) is evident at SSW. The interior slopes down to SSE from the fairly level N third, levelling out again in the S third. There is a souterrain (SL046-032002-) in the W half of the interior. Immediately outside the wall at S is a sod-covered stony rise (6m N-S; c. 10m E-W) defined by a low uneven scarp (H 0.5m). Stones and boulders protrude from the edge of this platform, some of which may be bedrock. A narrower (Wth 2-3m; H 0.3m) continuation of this rise is evident S-SW immediately outside the cashel wall.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On top of a small conical knoll, in mature woodland within the Coolavin estate. A circular area (27m N-S; 27.3m E-W) enclosed by a substantial drystone wall (Wth 4.3m; int. H 2m; ext. H 2.5m) incorporating in its internal face flights of stairs, terracing, a mural chamber and a souterrain (SL046-034002-). The wall (Wth 5m) of roughly coursed sandstone slabs and blocks survives to a height of 2m with a maximum external height of 2.5m at N dictated by the steeper fall of ground on that side of the knoll. The lower courses of the external wall-face incorporate very large blocks of stone. A plain entrance passage (Wth 1.75m) with traces of stone paving extends through the wall at SE. Flanking the S side of the entrance is a flight of steps, beginning at a height of 0.7m above the base of the wall, leading to the top of the wall. At SSE a flight of steps rises to a narrow terrace or wall-walk (Wth 0.57m; 0.7m below top to wall) that follows the curve of the wall to SSW where it slopes down gently and ends in a short dilapidated series of steps. The wall-walk begins again almost immediately and continues to W ending in a paired arrangement of lateral steps. The N flight of the pair leads to a very short length of wall-walk ending in a second pair of stairs. At the base of the wall between the two pairs of stairs there is a low lintelled opening giving access to a mural passage or souterrain (SL046-034002-). There is another flight of steps to the top of the wall at NNW and paired flights at NE. Flanking the N side of the entrance a low lintelled opening (Wth 0.72m; H 0.55m; T1.1m) gives access to the S end of a lintelled mural chamber (L 3.15m N-S; Wth 0.85m; H 1.43m). The interior of the cashel is level and raised above the base of the wall. An opening to a second souterrain (SL046-034003-) occurs in the surface in the W half of the interior. A trench-like depression (Wth c. 1.5m; D 0.6m), contiguous with the internal wall-face, dug to the base of the wall, is continuous around the circuit of the interior, except for short breaks at SW and at W in the vicinity of the souterrains (SL046-034002-; SL046-034003-). According to Harbison (1992, 291), 'this fine stone fort ... was partially rebuilt in the 19th century'.
This is a National Monument in state care (no. 159).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
At the W end of Inch Island in Lough Gara, on a gentle W-facing slope, above and immediately to N of a steep natural shelf which forms the division between agricultural land and the lakeshore stony grazing. A subcircular area (int. diam. 36m N-S; 39m E-W) enclosed by an earth and stone bank (Wth 5.5-7.5m; int. H 1.4m; ext. H 1.4m). An external flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.5m) is evident W-SE. The bank has several gaps (Wth c. 1.5m), all of which are recent, and has some whitethorn bushes growing on it. The entrance (Wth 1.3m) is at ESE. The interior is largely covered with mature ash trees, some of which have fallen. A raised area (25m N-S; 12m E-W; H 0.6m) in the E half of the interior abuts the bank at E. There is a possible souterrain (SL047-001002-) in the bank at SSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In Lough Gara, on the S shore of Inch island, c. 100m E of another crannog (SL047-003----). It is connected to the shore via a causeway at N, but in winter is surrounded by water. It is sparsely covered with grass though there is some overgrowth on the N portion. A low-cairn crannog (11.1m N-S; 12.2m E-W; H 1.2m above the marl lake-bed), the unstable surface of which mainly consists of a dense concentration of angular flagstones (diam. c. 0.4m). The stones are loosely packed with very little soil fill between them. The cairn slopes gently down into the lake and seems to be surrounded by a submerged plateau of flagstones. A possible hut site (SL047-004002-) is visible 9.4m to N. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 017)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, at Castle Point which is the W end of a narrow island close to the E shore of Lough Gara. An oval platform (21m x 18.5m; H c. 0.7m) blocks off the end of the Point. The platform is defined by a stony bank (int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.2m) with an external fosse (Wth 3m; D 1m) on the inland side N-S. On the E side of the platform are the fragmentary remains of a rectangular stone-built structure (int. dims. 7.3m x 4.7m) which has been largely reduced to a sod-covered mound of rubble. Some external wall facing, which includes blocks of dressed limestone, is evident, however, on its S side. A drystone field boundary wall (T 1.25m; H 0.3m) extends from the S side of the rubble mound to the lakeshore, blocking off the W end of the island. This is a castle of the O'Garas.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). In this instance the entry has been revised and updated in the light of recent research.

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'House Site'. Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. In the centre of a rath (SL047-010001-). The remains of a rectangular stone-built house with collapsed walls (T 2.2m; H 0.8m). The sunken interior is divided into two rooms (the W room: 6.3m N-S; 6.3m E-W; the E room: 6.3m N-S; 5.3m E-W) by a crossing wall which has a connecting door ope at its S end. The W room has opes at the E end of the N and S walls, that in the S wall possibly being the entrance ope. This is likely to be post-1700 AD in date. It is mentioned under the record for the rath.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
On the S side of Derrymore Island, in a water-meadow below an earlier shoreline of Lough Gara. A low-cairn crannog (14.3m N-S; 15.2m E-W; H 1.3m above the meadow) of which the main surface material is loosely packed stone. There is a mid-cairn (3m N-S; 3m E-W), with distinct edges, consisting of a dense concentration of rounded to subangular sandstone stones (diam. 0.1-0.2m). The edges of the mid-cairn are distinct. It is surrounded by a sloping stone plateau (c. 8.1m N-S; 2-4m E-W). The berm consists of angular stones (diam. c. 0.2-0.3m) slightly more firmly set into the ground. The edge of the crannog is well defined, with the N portion more built up and the SW portion more spread out. Two wooden posts are evident on the E portion. Most of it is overgrown with nettles, briars and small trees and some stones are covered with black moss. This is a low-cairn crannog with some attributes of a high-cairn crannog, mainly the presence of the mid-cairn. Drumlins block the view N-S. This crannog is amongst a group of eight possible crannogs (see SL047-012002-; SL047-012003-; SL047-012004-; SL047-012005-; SL047-012006-; SL047-012007-; SL047-012008-; SL047-012009-) in the small bay between Derrymore Island and Derrybeg townland. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 023)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In a wet meadow, on the N side of a bay below an earlier shoreline of Lough Gara and 33m W of a possible crannog (SL047-012003-). A grass-covered stone platform (9.4m N-S; 8.6m E-W; H 0.5m above the meadow) of scattered sandstone and limestone stones (diam. 0.2-0.5m), most of which are well set into the ground. The platform stands out slightly from the earlier shoreline and also materially from the relatively stone-free meadow. This is the most westerly of a group of eight smaller crannogs recorded by Cross (1953). It is one of a group of eight possible crannogs (see SL047-012003-; SL047-012004-; SL047-012005-; SL047-012006-; SL047-012007-; SL047-012008-; SL047-012009-) and one crannog (SL047-012001-) in the small bay between Derrymore Island and Derrybeg townland. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 024).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

The S portion of the site is an irregular mound (6m N-S; 9.6m E-W; max. H 0.51m above the meadow) that slopes down gently in all directions. The surfaces of both parts are grass-covered and somewhat uneven. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 041).

source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow, near an inlet of Lough Gara. Views are blocked to E, N and S by drumlins. An oval high-cairn crannog (26m N-S; 24m E-W; H 2.8m above the meadow). The grass-covered mid-cairn (10.4m N-S; 7.4m E-W) is located slightly off-centre to E. The edges of the mid-cairn slope gently down towards the surrounding plateau in all directions except to N, where there is a sharper drop. The plateau stretches out to N, W and S and consists of a dense concentration of loosely packed stones. It slopes gently towards the edges and is sparsely overgrown with ivy and flowers. Under the top layer of large stones, smaller shattered stones are visible, creating an uneven surface. The edge drops off distinctly in all directions and is very distinct in material. There is very little overspill of stones from the crannog. The vegetation consists of grass, large trees and bushes. (Cross 1953, fig. 1; Fredengren 2002, KILA 052)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On top of an 'altar' or penitential station (SL046-026002-), within the W half of Annagh graveyard (SL046-026001-). The upper surface of the altar is covered with a loose jumble of stones, mostly irregular but including several water-rolled cobbles. These cobbles are known locally as 'praying stones' (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney) and are similar to the 'Clocha Breacha' (Cursing stones) on Inishmurray island, county Sligo (see Harbison 1991, fig. 37).

source_data.original_text:
In the shallow waters of Lough Gara, surrounded by rushes and reeds. There are no views of the open lake due to the surrounding drumlins. A small stone platform (3.8m N-S; 3.4m E-W; max. H 0.35m above the lake-bed) consisting of limestone and sandstone boulders (diam. c. 0.2m) loosely set in the water. There is a medium density of stones in the site body. The edge is distinct in material, but as it consists of these small boulders it is quite irregular in shape. There is a concentration of stones extending out from the NW edge towards the deeper waters, probably overspill from the crannog or a small causeway. It consists of a stretch of loose stones (L 5.6m; Wth 0.4-0.5m) resting on the lake mud. About 1m to SW is another drier area (L 7.2m; Wth 4m) along the W edges of which is a diffuse spread of both angular stones and shattered and fire-cracked stones. According to local information, antlers were found on this site. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 038)


The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a wet meadow, below the old shoreline of Lough Gara. A low oval grass-covered mound (9.9m N-S; 12.4m E-W; max. H 0.72m above the meadow) with an even surface. Occasional small stones (diam. 0.2m) protrude through the grass, especially on the W portion. The edges slope gradually and are quite distinct in material. This crannog is surrounded by a series of three oblong mounds (43.2m x 9.5m; 41.5m x 10.5m; 24.2m x 12m) consisting of shattered or fire-cracked stones enclosing an area 31m in internal diameter. Marked by Cross (1953, fig. 1) as one of a group of seven sites in the N half of Ross townland. (Fredengren 2002, KILA 040)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, below the old shoreline of Lough Gara, on the N shore of Ross townland. source_data.original_text:
In Moygara Castle (SL044-052001-). This is an architectural fragment, a limestone keystone which is lying on the ground near the gate tower of the castle. It has a carving on its outside face but this is now almost worn beyond recognition. The carving appears to be two figures facing each. Another keystone (SL044-052002-) lies nearby and it has an equally worn carving of a single figure holding something in its arms (SMR (1989) file). Neither of these carvings appear to be the figure of a sheela-na-gig, though Guest (1936, 111 and fig. 7) implies that one might be.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
Within a graveyard (SL046-026002-), located on a penitential station (MA046-026002-), named ‘Altar’ on the OS 6-inch maps. According to local information, a roughly circular stone (diam. approx. 0.4m) with a central circular hollow was traditionally kept on top of the penitential station. It may have been a bullaun stone, or possibly a stoup or font. Unusually, it had a lid or cap, which consisted of a smaller stone, hemispherical in shape, the flat side of which was placed over the central hollow of the large stone. These stones were stolen and their current whereabouts are unknown. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Clooncunny 2 | Logboat | Oak wood. Given by Lanting & Brindley (1996, 89) as 'found on bank of R. Boyle (1968). Several parts and pieces brought to NMI'. However, there is no Clooncunny townland in that part of the lake. If the location is as described, the only townland that fits and is in Sligo is Cuppanagh. Alternately, there is a river channel linking two parts of Lough Gara & this may be what the authors are referring to. Geo-location has been selected based on the second possibility as it remains in the Clooncunny Townland.
